diseases.name: White Spot Disease (Ichthyophthiriasis)

contagious.transmission: Direct life cycle without intermediate host: free-swimming theronts infect every fish in the tank. Introduced via new fish, plants, substrate, water and equipment; surviving fish can remain carriers.
contagious.notes: Highly contagious; often fatal if untreated.

diseases.description: Ichthyophthirius multifiliis is a large, single-celled ciliate and one of the most common parasites of freshwater fish worldwide. Its life cycle has three stages: the feeding trophont in the skin (the visible white spots), the dividing cyst on the substrate (tomont) and the free-swimming infective theront. A single cyst releases a very large number of theronts, so infestations spread explosively. The length of the cycle depends strongly on temperature. Because the parasite is protected in the skin and inside the cyst, medication only acts on the free-swimming stages – repeated treatments over several cycles are therefore necessary. Gill-only infections can be fatal without any visible spots.
generalSigns: White, salt- or semolina-like spots (up to approx. 1 mm) on skin, fins and gills
Before or alongside: rubbing against objects (flashing), increased mucus, clamped fins
Rapid breathing, loss of appetite, weight loss, lethargy
With gill-only infection no visible spots, but sudden deaths
keySigns: White spots like grains of salt
diseases.diagnosis: Suspected from the typical spots; confirmed by skin/gill smear under the microscope (large, horseshoe-shaped nucleus).

treatment.summary: Treat immediately; repeat treatments over the length of the life cycle, as only the free-swimming stages are susceptible.
steps: Treat fish in a quarantine tank if possible; never treat invertebrates along with them.
Use an approved ornamental fish remedy against Ichthyophthirius according to the package insert and repeat over several cycles.
Siphon the substrate and change water daily – this removes cysts from the bottom.
Raise the temperature slightly, only within the species' tolerance: the cycle runs faster and the susceptible stages appear sooner.
Remove activated carbon during treatment; aerate well.
Continue treating after the last visible spot until at least one further cycle is covered.

activeSubstances.notes: Effective against theronts; lowers oxygen levels – aerate strongly. Scaleless species are sensitive.
For ornamental fish only; not permitted in food-producing animals in the EU. Scaleless fish react sensitively.
Prolonged use is described by UF/IFAS; not all species and plants tolerate salt.
Risky in freshwater: toxicity rises sharply at low alkalinity (UF/IFAS FA008).

treatment.prognosis: Good with early, consistent treatment; poor with gill infection and late treatment.

prevention: Do not share equipment between tanks, or disinfect it

diseases.name: Velvet Disease (Piscinoodiniosis, 'Oodinium')

contagious.transmission: Direct life cycle similar to Ich: parasites drop off, divide and release free-swimming dinospores that infect new fish.
contagious.notes: Less common and usually less aggressive in freshwater than the marine form Amyloodinium.

diseases.description: Piscinoodinium is a parasitic dinoflagellate that attaches to skin and gills. The infestation appears as a fine, gold to rust-coloured dust that is much finer than the spots of white spot disease and is often only noticeable in oblique light. The life cycle resembles that of Ichthyophthirius; the free-swimming stages are the main target of medication. Heavy gill infestation causes respiratory distress and can be fatal.
generalSigns: Fine gold, rust or velvety coating on skin and fins (shine a torch at an angle)
Fish stay in oxygen-rich areas (filter outlet)
Loss of appetite, later skin peeling
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopic detection of pear-shaped to spherical parasites in skin or gill smears.

treatment.summary: Treat in a quarantine tank with an approved ornamental fish remedy against Oodinium; repeat, as only free stages are susceptible.
steps: Isolate affected fish; never treat invertebrates along with them.
Use an ornamental fish remedy against Oodinium (often copper-based) according to the package insert.
Darkening the tank is often recommended in practice because Piscinoodinium photosynthesises (practical advice, little scientific evidence).
Aerate well, change water, siphon the substrate.

activeSubstances.notes: Toxicity rises in soft water with low alkalinity (UF/IFAS FA008).
Supportive; usually insufficient on its own.

treatment.prognosis: Good if detected early; serious with heavy gill infestation.

recommendedMedications.name: Malachite green + methylene blue + ethacridine (combination product)
Sodium chloride (pure salt)

diseases.name: Skin and Gill Clouding by Protozoa (Costia, Chilodonella, Trichodina)

pathogen.scientificName: Ichthyobodo spp. (formerly Costia), Chilodonella spp., Trichodina spp.

contagious.transmission: Directly from fish to fish and via the water; many fish carry small numbers without disease, mass multiplication under stress and poor water conditions.
contagious.notes: Opportunistic parasites – an outbreak usually indicates a husbandry problem.

diseases.description: Several very small protozoa live on skin and gills and multiply massively in weakened fish, under high organic load and overstocking. They are invisible to the naked eye; only the fish's reaction is visible: a grey-bluish clouding of the skin due to excessive mucus production, flashing and respiratory distress. Chilodonella and Ichthyobodo can quickly cause high losses with heavy gill infestation. As the pathogens cannot be distinguished without a microscope, they are listed together here.
generalSigns: Rapid breathing, fish stay near the surface
diseases.diagnosis: Can only be reliably distinguished microscopically by skin and gill smears.

treatment.summary: Improve water quality and treat with an approved ornamental fish remedy against skin parasites.
steps: Generous water changes, siphon the substrate, check stocking.
Ornamental fish remedy against ectoparasites (e.g. formalin-based) according to the package insert, in a quarantine tank if invertebrates are present.
Eliminate the cause – without better husbandry the infestation will return.

activeSubstances.notes: Effective against Ichthyobodo, Chilodonella and Trichodina; aerate strongly.
Frequently used; tolerance depends on species.

treatment.prognosis: Good if the husbandry cause is eliminated.

prevention: Good water quality and appropriate stocking

diseases.name: Skin and Gill Flukes (Monogenea: Gyrodactylus, Dactylogyrus)

pathogen.scientificName: Gyrodactylus spp. (live-bearing, mainly skin), Dactylogyrus spp. (egg-laying, mainly gills)

contagious.transmission: Direct life cycle from fish to fish; Gyrodactylus gives birth to young directly on the host, Dactylogyrus lays eggs from which larvae hatch.
contagious.notes: Accumulate in aquariums because of the closed system.

diseases.description: Monogeneans are flatworms a few tenths of a millimetre long that hold on to skin or gills with hooks and feed on mucus and skin cells. Usually harmless in the wild, they multiply strongly in aquariums. Gyrodactylus is live-bearing and multiplies very quickly on the skin; Dactylogyrus mainly infests the gills and lays eggs that are protected against many medications. The damaged skin is an entry point for bacteria.
generalSigns: Flared gill covers, rapid breathing, pale or swollen gills
Cloudy skin, frayed fins, small skin lesions
predisposingFactors: New fish, especially from mass breeding
diseases.diagnosis: Skin or gill smear under the microscope (hooks; in Gyrodactylus embryos visible inside the worm).

treatment.summary: Anthelmintic (usually praziquantel) according to the package insert; with Dactylogyrus repeat after about a week to catch hatched larvae.
steps: Use an ornamental fish remedy against skin and gill flukes.
Repeat the treatment according to the manufacturer for egg-laying species (Dactylogyrus).
Improve water quality, check stocking.

activeSubstances.notes: Common active ingredient in ornamental fish remedies; check tolerance for invertebrates with the manufacturer.
Alternative for skin infestation.
Described for Gyrodactylus of guppies; species-dependent.

diseases.name: Red Intestinal Worms (Camallanosis)

contagious.transmission: Females release live larvae. In the aquarium, Camallanus cotti has been shown to transmit directly from fish to fish without an intermediate host; larvae survive more than three weeks in the tank.
contagious.notes: Spreads over generations in a closed aquarium.

diseases.description: Camallanus are small red roundworms that attach to the intestinal wall and suck blood. Infestation is most obvious when the reddish worms protrude from the anus, especially after feeding. Lightly infested fish show hardly any symptoms; heavy infestation leads to weight loss, a swollen abdomen and deaths. Livebearers are particularly often affected, but also barbs, cichlids and rainbowfish.
generalSigns: Red, thread-like worms protruding from the anus (especially after feeding)
Weight loss despite eating, sunken or swollen abdomen
predisposingFactors: New fish, especially livebearers from mass breeding
diseases.diagnosis: Visible worms at the anus; otherwise faecal examination by a veterinarian.

treatment.summary: Anthelmintic against roundworms (levamisole or benzimidazoles such as fenbendazole/flubendazole); repeat after about 2–3 weeks.
steps: Treat all fish in the tank, not only visibly infested ones.
Apply the remedy according to the package insert (bath or food); according to ANGFA levamisole acts on free larvae and parasitic stages.
After treatment, siphon the substrate thoroughly and change water.
Second treatment to catch regrowing stages.
Remove invertebrates first (benzimidazoles are considered harmful to snails).

activeSubstances.notes: Legal status depends on the product; obtain via specialist trade/veterinarian.
Harmful to snails.

treatment.prognosis: Good with complete treatment; severely emaciated fish often do not recover.

prevention: Quarantine new fish and watch the anus

diseases.name: Neon Tetra Disease (Pleistophorosis)

contagious.transmission: Via spores: fish eat dead or sick conspecifics or spore-containing faeces. Healthy-looking fish can be carriers and only fall ill under stress.
contagious.notes: Not restricted to neon tetras – proven to be transmissible to zebra danios, among others.

diseases.description: Pleistophora hyphessobryconis infects the skeletal muscle. The spores form large clusters that appear as white, glassy patches under the skin and destroy the muscle. The type host is the neon tetra, but the pathogen infects many aquarium fish; Sanders et al. (2010) transmitted it experimentally from neon tetras to zebrafish. No effective treatment is known; infected fish usually die.
generalSigns: Whitish, glassy discolouration of the musculature (often on the back, colour stripe fades or is interrupted)
Jerky, uncoordinated swimming, separates from the shoal
predisposingFactors: Eating dead fish in the tank
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopic spore detection in muscle tissue by a laboratory; externally only a suspicion.

treatment.summary: No effective treatment known – humanely euthanise and remove sick fish.
steps: Remove sick fish immediately and euthanise humanely before they die and are eaten.
Never leave dead fish in the tank.
Clean tank and equipment thoroughly after an outbreak; spores are resistant.
Monitor the stock; do not add new fish until no further cases occur.

prevention: Buy healthy animals from good breeders

recommendedMedications.name: Clove oil (eugenol)
recommendedMedications.legalStatusLabel: not a medicine – freely available (shops, pharmacy, drugstore)

diseases.name: Guppy Disease (Tetrahymenosis)

contagious.transmission: Via the water; the pathogen penetrates the skin and can spread systemically to muscle and organs. Stress promotes infection.
contagious.notes: Major problem in guppy mass breeding.

diseases.description: Tetrahymena is a normally free-living ciliate that infects the skin, muscles and internal organs of weakened fish, especially guppies. Unlike pure skin parasites it invades the tissue, which is why external treatments hardly work in advanced infections. Experimentally, niclosamide in the food reduced mortality (Pimenta Leibowitz et al. 2010); there is no approved remedy.
generalSigns: Whitish patches or coatings on skin and fins
Raised scales, pop-eye when the eyes are affected
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopically (motile, pear-shaped ciliates in tissue or smear).

treatment.summary: Hardly treatable once systemic; isolate sick fish, improve husbandry, consult a veterinarian.
steps: Isolate sick fish immediately.
Improve water quality, reduce organic load.
Consult a fish veterinarian for therapy (experimental substances only via a veterinarian).

activeSubstances.notes: Studies only; no approved ornamental fish remedy.

recommendedMedications.name: Clove oil (eugenol)

diseases.name: Columnaris (Cotton Mouth, Saddleback)

contagious.transmission: Via the water and direct contact; the bacterium survives in water and mud. Healthy-looking fish can be carriers from previous outbreaks.
contagious.notes: Can kill many fish acutely within hours to days.

diseases.description: Flavobacterium columnare causes skin, fin and gill infections, especially in warm-water fish. Typical are whitish-grey to yellowish, cotton-like coatings on the mouth, which are often mistaken for fungus, as well as pale, saddle-shaped patches on the back. The course ranges from chronic to acute with high mortality and depends strongly on the virulence of the strain. Injuries, poor water quality and high organic load favour outbreaks.
generalSigns: Whitish-grey to yellowish coating on the mouth ('cotton mouth'), disintegration of the lips
Pale, saddle-like patches on the back
predisposingFactors: High organic load, poor water quality
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopically (long, gliding rods arranged in columns); confirmed by culture on special media.

treatment.summary: Act fast: improve water quality immediately and involve a fish veterinarian; antibiotics require a prescription.
steps: Isolate sick fish, generous water changes.
Consult a fish veterinarian for diagnosis and possible antibiotic therapy.
Reduce organic load and stocking.

diseases.name: Fin Rot and Bacterial Ulcers (Aeromonas, Pseudomonas)

pathogen.scientificName: Aeromonas spp. (incl. A. hydrophila), Pseudomonas spp.

contagious.transmission: The bacteria occur in every aquarium and mainly cause disease in weakened or injured fish. Transmission via the water.
contagious.notes: Aeromonas can cause intestinal and wound infections in humans – observe hygiene.

diseases.description: Motile aeromonads and pseudomonads are part of the normal aquatic flora. They become a problem when fish are weakened by poor water, stress or injuries (e.g. from fin nippers). Locally they cause fin rot and skin ulcers; if the infection spreads through the body, haemorrhages, dropsy and pop-eye occur. The bacterial infection is often a consequence of another problem (parasites, husbandry errors).
generalSigns: Frayed, milky fin edges, fins melt away
Red pinpoint haemorrhages, reddened fin bases
diseases.diagnosis: Clinical; reliable pathogen identification and sensitivity testing by bacteriological examination at a fish veterinarian.

treatment.summary: Eliminate the cause (water quality, tankmates); if it progresses, a fish veterinarian with sensitivity testing.
steps: Check water parameters, change water, maintain the filter.
Separate fin nippers.
Mild fin rot often heals with better husbandry alone.
With ulcers, haemorrhages or spreading, consult a fish veterinarian – antibiotics only after sensitivity testing.

activeSubstances.notes: Antibiotics and other antimicrobial veterinary medicines (e.g. metronidazole) have required a veterinary prescription throughout the EU since 28 January 2022 (Art. 34 Regulation (EU) 2019/6) – obtain only via a (fish) veterinarian.

treatment.prognosis: Good if the cause is eliminated early; poor with systemic infection.

prevention: No fin nippers with long-finned species

diseases.name: Fish Tuberculosis (Mycobacteriosis)

pathogen.scientificName: Mycobacterium marinum, M. fortuitum, M. chelonae and others

contagious.transmission: Via eating infected fish, faeces and water; the bacteria also live in filter media and biofilms.
contagious.notes: ZOONOSIS: can cause slow-healing skin nodules ('fish tank granuloma') in humans through small skin injuries. Wear gloves when working in the tank, especially with open wounds or a weakened immune system.

diseases.description: Mycobacteriosis is a chronic, wasting infection in which nodules (granulomas) form in the spleen, kidney and liver. Fish do not get true tuberculosis; the term is outdated. The disease progresses slowly over weeks to months, often affects older fish and can affect any fish species. There are no non-lethal tests for live fish; diagnosis is usually made post mortem by a laboratory.
generalSigns: Individual deaths over a long period
diseases.diagnosis: Laboratory examination (Ziehl-Neelsen staining or PCR) via a fish veterinarian.

treatment.summary: No reliable cure. Humanely euthanise sick fish; with mass infection restart and disinfect the tank.
steps: Remove suspicious fish and have them examined.
Remove dead fish immediately.
If confirmed: monitor the stock, possibly dismantle and disinfect the tank completely.
Wear gloves, wash hands.
treatment.prognosis: Poor; mycobacteria are naturally resistant to many antibiotics.

recommendedMedications.name: Clove oil (eugenol)
recommendedMedications.legalStatusLabel: not a medicine – freely available (shops, pharmacy, drugstore)

diseases.name: Dwarf Gourami Iridovirus (DGIV / ISKNV)
synonyms: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus

contagious.transmission: Via the water; experimentally transmissible to other fish species (Murray cod, 90 % mortality). Infection also detected in farmed platies.
contagious.notes: Incurable; latently infected fish can spread the virus.

diseases.description: A megalocytivirus that destroys the spleen, kidney and other organs. Dwarf gouramis from the trade are frequently infected. Go & Whittington (2006) showed that the virus from dwarf gouramis is transmissible to other species; Rimmer et al. also detected it in farmed platies. Sick fish usually show non-specific symptoms and die within a short time.
diseases.diagnosis: PCR or histology via a fish veterinarian.

treatment.summary: No treatment possible. Humanely euthanise sick fish, disinfect the tank.
steps: Isolate or humanely euthanise sick fish.
Do not pass on any fish from the tank.
Disinfect tank and equipment after losses.
Never release fish into the wild.

prevention: Buy dwarf gouramis only from trustworthy, ideally tested sources

diseases.name: Lymphocystis ('Cauliflower Disease')

contagious.transmission: Horizontally via the water and direct contact; surviving fish can remain symptom-free carriers.
contagious.notes: Usually benign and self-limiting.

diseases.description: The lymphocystis virus causes individual connective tissue cells of the skin to swell enormously. White to pink, granular nodules reminiscent of cauliflower develop, mostly on fins and skin. The disease affects more than 125 fish species in fresh and salt water, is usually chronic and self-limiting – the nodules often regress after weeks to months. Stress promotes outbreaks; secondary infections are possible.
generalSigns: White to pink, granular nodules (cauliflower-like) on fins and skin
Rarely nodules on gills or mouth with feeding/breathing problems
diseases.diagnosis: Typical appearance; confirmation by histology (greatly enlarged cells) or PCR.

treatment.summary: No specific therapy. Optimise husbandry; the nodules usually regress on their own.
steps: Isolate the affected fish to avoid infection.
Improve water quality, reduce stress.
If impaired (mouth, gills), consult a fish veterinarian (surgical removal possible).

diseases.name: Fungal Infection (Saprolegniasis)

contagious.transmission: Spores are present in practically every water body; mainly injured or weakened fish and dead eggs are affected.
contagious.notes: Usually a secondary disease, not a primary epidemic.

diseases.description: Saprolegnia is a water mould that grows on dead tissue and spreads from there to living tissue. White to grey, cotton-like threads develop on wounds, fins or the mouth. Untreated, the infestation spreads and can be fatal by disturbing the salt-water balance. Cool temperatures favour Saprolegnia ('winter fungus'). Distinguishing it from columnaris, which also looks cotton-like but is bacterial, is important.
generalSigns: White to grey, cotton-like threads on wounds, fins or mouth
Threads turn greenish/brownish from trapped dirt
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopically (branched, non-septate hyphae); distinguishing from columnaris is important.

treatment.summary: Eliminate the underlying cause (injury, husbandry) and treat with an approved ornamental fish remedy against fungal infection.
steps: Clarify the cause of the wounds (tankmates, decoration).
Ornamental fish remedy against fungal infection according to the package insert.
Improve water quality; do not keep cold-water species too cool.

activeSubstances.substance: Ornamental fish remedies against fungal infection (e.g. malachite green based)
activeSubstances.notes: Toxic to shrimp, crayfish and snails – never use in a tank with invertebrates.
Supportive; species-dependent.

diseases.name: Dropsy (Syndrome)
synonyms: Malawi bloat (in cichlids of Lake Malawi/Tanganyika)

pathogen.scientificName: incl. bacterial infections, organ damage (kidney), viral infections, feeding errors

contagious.transmission: Contagious only if there is an infectious underlying cause (e.g. bacterial septicaemia).
contagious.notes: Not a disease in its own right – clarify the cause.

diseases.description: Dropsy is a symptom: fluid accumulates in the body cavity and tissues, usually because the kidneys or circulation fail. Causes are frequently bacterial infections, but also viral infections, organ damage and husbandry errors. In herbivorous cichlids (especially Tropheus) a similar clinical picture is called 'Malawi bloat' and is linked to protein-rich feeding and stress; the exact cause has not been scientifically established.
generalSigns: Lethargy, refusal of food, whitish faeces
diseases.diagnosis: Cause to be clarified by a fish veterinarian (bacteriology, laboratory examination).

treatment.summary: Isolate, improve husbandry and have the cause clarified; antibiotics only via a veterinarian. Humanely euthanise advanced cases.
steps: Isolate the fish.
Check and improve water quality.
Consult a fish veterinarian.
For Tropheus/aufwuchs grazers: purely plant-based, high-fibre diet; never add new fish to established groups.

diseases.name: Hole-in-the-Head Disease (Spironucleosis, 'Hexamitiasis')

pathogen.scientificName: Spironucleus vortens (formerly often referred to as Hexamita)

contagious.transmission: Via the faeces of infected fish (intestinal parasite); systemic spread in weakened fish.
contagious.notes: Many fish carry Spironucleus in the gut without falling ill.

diseases.description: Spironucleus vortens lives in the gut of many cichlids. Paull & Matthews (2001) isolated the pathogen from the kidney, liver, spleen and head lesions of discus with hole-in-the-head disease and proposed it as a possible cause that spreads through the body from the gut. In a Thai study, 90 % of angelfish, 75 % of oscars and 61 % of blue mbunas were infected, but no Siamese fighting fish. Husbandry factors (nitrate, diet) are considered contributing causes.
generalSigns: Small holes or pits on the head and along the lateral line
Weight loss, dark colouration, refusal of food
predisposingFactors: High nitrate levels, infrequent water changes
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopic detection in faeces or lesion smears.

treatment.summary: Significantly improve water quality; treatment with metronidazole (prescription-only) via a fish veterinarian.
steps: Frequent large water changes, lower nitrate.
Varied, high-quality diet.
Consult a fish veterinarian for diagnosis and metronidazole therapy (effective in vitro: Sangmaneedet & Smith 1999).

activeSubstances.notes: Antibiotics and other antimicrobial veterinary medicines (e.g. metronidazole) have required a veterinary prescription throughout the EU since 28 January 2022 (Art. 34 Regulation (EU) 2019/6) – obtain only via a (fish) veterinarian.

treatment.prognosis: Good with early treatment; scars may remain.

recommendedMedications.name: Metronidazole
recommendedMedications.roleLabel: only as prescribed by a veterinarian

diseases.name: Crayfish Plague

contagious.transmission: Via free-swimming zoospores in the water, especially on death and moulting of infected animals. North American crayfish are often symptom-free carriers.
contagious.notes: Fatal to European crayfish. Shrimp can also carry and transmit the pathogen.

diseases.description: Since the 19th century, crayfish plague has wiped out a large part of Europe's crayfish populations. North American species share an evolutionary history with the pathogen and usually carry it without falling ill. Screening of ornamental crayfish from the trade in Germany and the Czech Republic found A. astaci DNA in 27 % of the batches examined (Mrugała et al. 2015); further traded species were confirmed as carriers (Panteleit et al. 2017). Freshwater shrimp such as Macrobrachium dayanum can also become infected and transmit the pathogen to noble crayfish (Svoboda et al. 2014; NeoBiota 2020).
generalSigns: Sometimes brownish to black patches (melanisation) on joints, carapace or tail fan
In susceptible crayfish: restlessness, staggering, mass deaths
predisposingFactors: Keeping together with North American species
diseases.diagnosis: Molecular (qPCR) – not reliably detectable externally.

treatment.summary: No treatment. The key is to prevent spread.
steps: NEVER release crayfish, shrimp or tank water into natural waters or garden ponds.
Do not dispose of aquarium water into natural waters.
Do not use equipment for both crayfish tanks and natural waters.
Dispose of dead animals with household waste.

prevention: Do not keep together with native crayfish

diseases.name: Porcelain Disease (Microsporidiosis in Crustaceans)

pathogen.scientificName: incl. Thelohania spp. and other microsporidia

contagious.transmission: Via spores, mainly by eating dead infected animals.
contagious.notes: Microsporidia have been detected in feral Neocaridina populations in Europe.

diseases.description: Microsporidia infect the musculature of crustaceans; the tissue becomes opaque and porcelain-white. Affected animals become sluggish and die. No treatment is known. Several microsporidian species have been detected in feral Neocaridina davidi populations (Parasite 2025).
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopically (spores in the muscle) by a laboratory.

treatment.summary: No treatment known. Remove affected animals immediately.
steps: Remove milky-white animals immediately.
Do not leave dead animals in the tank.
Do not pass on animals from affected stocks.

diseases.name: Scutariella Infestation (Flatworms on Shrimp)

contagious.transmission: From shrimp to shrimp; eggs are laid in the gill chamber. Introduced to Europe with trade shrimp.
contagious.notes: Whether commensal or parasite is debated; in large numbers they stress the shrimp.

diseases.description: Scutariella japonica are tiny, white, finger-shaped worms that live mainly on the head and in the gill chamber of shrimp of the family Atyidae. Maciaszek et al. (2021) recorded them for the first time in Europe on feral Neocaridina davidi. In small numbers they are considered of little harm; heavy infestation can cause stress and oxygen deficiency.
generalSigns: Tiny white, finger-shaped worms on the head or rostrum
diseases.diagnosis: Easily visible with a magnifying glass.

treatment.summary: Short baths are used in practice; efficacy and tolerance are hardly studied scientifically. With light infestation, observe.
steps: Inspect new shrimp with a magnifying glass during quarantine.
With heavy infestation seek expert advice; treatments cautiously and only in a separate container.

diseases.name: Bell Animalcule Growth (Vorticella, Epistylis, Zoothamnium)

pathogen.scientificName: Vorticella spp., Epistylis spp., Zoothamnium spp.

contagious.transmission: Present in almost every aquarium; occur in masses on animals under high organic load.
contagious.notes: Indicator of excessive organic load.

diseases.description: Sessile ciliates settle on the carapace of shrimp and crayfish. They feed on bacteria in the water and are mainly an indicator of high organic load. In large numbers, especially on the gills, they impair breathing and moulting. They are shed during moulting. Vorticellidae were recorded together with Scutariella on Neocaridina in Europe (Maciaszek et al. 2021).
generalSigns: Whitish, fuzzy coating on carapace, legs or eye stalks
keySigns: White, fuzzy coating on the carapace
predisposingFactors: High organic load, infrequent water changes
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopically (bell-shaped cells on stalks).

treatment.summary: Reduce organic load; the animals usually shed the coating at the next moult.
steps: Feed less, remove leftovers.
Regular water changes.
Maintain the filter.

diseases.name: Poisoning by Copper and Fish Medication (Invertebrates)

pathogen.scientificName: Copper, malachite green, formalin and many other substances

contagious.transmission: No transmission.

diseases.description: Most invertebrates are highly sensitive to copper and many fish medications. According to UF/IFAS, copper is toxic to snails and most zooplankton; in marine systems invertebrates should only be returned at no more than 0.01 mg/L, ideally 0 mg/L copper. Many other fish medications are also unsuitable for invertebrates – the manufacturer's information is decisive.
generalSigns: Shrimp swim frantically, fall over, moulting problems
predisposingFactors: Treating fish in the community tank
diseases.diagnosis: Temporal link with the dose; copper test.

treatment.summary: Immediately large water changes, activated carbon or copper-binding filter media; move surviving animals to clean water.
steps: Large water change.
Use activated carbon or special adsorbers.
In future always treat fish in a separate quarantine tank.
Before using any new remedy with invertebrates, check the manufacturer's information on tolerance.

prevention: Do not use tanks with a copper history for invertebrates

diseases.name: Fish Lice (Argulosis)

contagious.transmission: The lice swim freely from fish to fish; eggs are laid on decoration and plants. Usually introduced via pond fish, live food or wild water.
contagious.notes: Can transmit other pathogens while sucking blood.

diseases.description: Fish lice are flat, oval crustaceans visible to the naked eye (about 5 mm) that hold on to the skin and fins with suckers and suck blood. Inflammation and ulcers develop at the feeding sites, through which bacteria enter. Pond and cold-water fish are most frequently affected; in tropical aquariums they are rare, usually introduced with pond fish or live food.
generalSigns: Flat, disc-shaped, translucent parasites (approx. 5 mm) on skin or fins that can move
Reddened feeding sites, ulcers, raised scales
keySigns: Flat, oval lice on the skin
predisposingFactors: Pond fish, live food from natural waters
diseases.diagnosis: Visible to the naked eye or with a magnifying glass.

treatment.summary: Approved ornamental fish remedy against parasitic crustaceans (e.g. emamectin or diflubenzuron product); repeat after about 3 weeks to catch newly hatched lice.
steps: Carefully remove individual lice with tweezers.
Treat the tank or pond with an approved remedy against parasitic crustaceans.
Repeat the treatment according to the manufacturer (eggs survive the first treatment).
Remove invertebrates first – these remedies kill all crustaceans.

activeSubstances.notes: Freely available ornamental fish remedy (e.g. sera med Professional Argulol).
Ornamental fish remedy for garden ponds (e.g. OASE AntiArgulus).

prevention: No live food from fish-bearing waters

diseases.name: Anchor Worms (Lernaeosis)

contagious.transmission: Free larval stages infect new fish; the females burrow into the tissue with an anchor.
contagious.notes: Successfully treated fish may develop some resistance (UF/IFAS).

diseases.description: Anchor worms are not worms but copepod crustaceans. The female burrows deep into the tissue with an anchor-shaped head and hangs out of the skin as a 1–3 cm long thread with two egg sacs. The puncture sites become strongly inflamed. Cyprinids such as goldfish are particularly often affected, but many other freshwater fish are also susceptible.
generalSigns: Thread-like parasites (1–3 cm) hanging from the skin, often with two egg sacs at the end
Flashing, weight loss with heavy infestation
keySigns: Threads with egg sacs hanging from the skin
diseases.diagnosis: Visible to the naked eye; microscope for confirmation.

treatment.summary: Approved remedy against parasitic crustaceans; repeat treatment. Pull out only carefully, as the anchor can break off in the tissue.
steps: Isolate the fish.
Ornamental fish remedy against parasitic crustaceans according to the package insert; repeat according to the manufacturer.
Watch the puncture sites (secondary infections).
Remove invertebrates first.

activeSubstances.notes: According to the manufacturer, kills anchor worms within three days.
Pond product.
According to UF/IFAS kills larvae; adults may survive.

treatment.prognosis: Usually good; chronic infestation weakens the fish.

prevention: No live food from fish-bearing waters

diseases.name: Tapeworms (Cestodiasis)

pathogen.scientificName: incl. Bothriocephalus spp. and other tapeworms

contagious.transmission: Usually via intermediate hosts (small crustaceans, live food); rarely passed on in aquariums without intermediate hosts.
contagious.notes: Common in wild-caught fish.

diseases.description: Tapeworms live in the gut or body cavity and deprive the fish of nutrients. They are usually not visible from the outside; signs are weight loss despite eating and a swollen abdomen. Occasionally white, flat worm segments appear at the anus or in the faeces. According to the manufacturer, praziquantel-containing ornamental fish remedies are also effective against tapeworms.
generalSigns: Occasionally white, flat worm segments at the anus or in the faeces
keySigns: white worm segments at the anus
diseases.diagnosis: Faecal examination by a fish veterinarian.

treatment.summary: Praziquantel product according to the package insert.
steps: Treat with praziquantel (tapeworm dosage according to the manufacturer).
Siphon faeces and debris.
Treat wild-caught fish preventively in quarantine.

activeSubstances.notes: Freely available (e.g. sera med Professional Tremazol).

prevention: No live food from fish-bearing waters

diseases.name: Capillaria Worms (Capillariasis)

contagious.transmission: Via eggs in the faeces; direct transmission possible in aquariums.
contagious.notes: According to the manufacturer mainly in angelfish and discus.

diseases.description: Capillaria are very thin roundworms in the gut. Unlike Camallanus they do not protrude visibly from the anus. Infested fish lose weight, pass whitish, slimy faeces and darken. According to the manufacturer, a freely available emamectin-based ornamental fish remedy is particularly effective against Camallanus and Capillaria.
diseases.diagnosis: Faecal examination (eggs) by a fish veterinarian.

steps: Treat all fish in the tank.
Siphon faeces and debris thoroughly.
Repeat the treatment.
Remove invertebrates first.

diseases.name: Ammonia and Nitrite Poisoning

pathogen.scientificName: Ammonia (NH3) and nitrite (NO2⁻) from the nitrogen cycle

contagious.transmission: No transmission.
contagious.notes: Usually affects all animals in a tank at the same time.

diseases.description: Ammonia is produced from fish waste and broken down by bacteria via nitrite to nitrate. In newly set-up tanks, after filter failure or with overstocking, ammonia and nitrite accumulate. According to UF/IFAS, nitrite is toxic from as little as 0.10 mg/L; it converts the blood pigment into methaemoglobin, which no longer transports oxygen (brown blood disease). Free ammonia (NH3) is more toxic the higher the pH and temperature.
generalSigns: Many animals affected at the same time
Rapid breathing, fish stay at the surface
Sudden deaths, especially in new tanks
diseases.diagnosis: Water test (ammonium, nitrite).

treatment.summary: Immediately change water, stop feeding, check the filter. For nitrite in freshwater, chloride (salt) protects: according to UF/IFAS 10 mg/L chloride per 1 mg/L nitrite.
steps: Immediately make a large water change (same temperature).
Stop or strongly reduce feeding for 1–2 days.
Check the filter, do not wash it out.
Freshwater: add chloride (table salt) at a ratio of 10 mg/L chloride to 1 mg/L nitrite (UF/IFAS FA16) – check salt-sensitive plants/species first.
Measure daily until ammonium and nitrite are no longer detectable.

activeSubstances.notes: Ratio 10:1 chloride to nitrite (UF/IFAS FA16).

treatment.prognosis: Good with quick action; severely damaged animals can still die days later.

recommendedMedications.name: Sodium chloride (pure salt)
